newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Novartis impresses analysts with outlook.
newsitem.headline: Novartis impresses analysts with outlook.

text.p: Novartis AG on Wednesday presented its research programme to an eager audience of analysts prompting many to reconfirm buy recommendations and increase already bullish growth forecasts.

"I think the main message I took home was that we can be very confident that the company can sustain very high growth rates not only in the next five years, but also beyond that," said Michael Sjoestroem at Pictet & Cie said .
"The company had been talking about eight percent underlying growth (in pharmaceutical sales) but it now seems that it will be 10 percent," said UBS analyst Birgit Kulhoff.

In a major presentation on Tuesday, the health sciences group told analysts that its post-merger integration process was still on target and that it had 11 products in the new drug pipeline which it expects to launch by the end of the decade.
Novartis executives said their goal was to introduce three commercially attractive products per year.

"The general view was that it (the presentation) was very positive. We are adjusting a few of our numbers upwards and we are maintaining our 'overweight' recommendation," said James Harding of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

He also said his target price for the stock was 2,400 Swiss francs by year-end. It was quoted at 2,147 in Wednesday mid-morning trading, up 29 from Tuesday's close. The stock began the year at about 1,460.
Novartis was formed last year through the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz AG. The merger created the second largest group in the industry after the British drug giant Glaxo Wellcome Plc.

"Some people thought Novartis was just a restructuring story," Kulhoff said. But she said the company was able to convince analysts that the prospects for their 75 development projects in progress were realistic.

Novartis chief executive Daniel Vasella said in a telephone interview on Tuesday that the most promising of products due for launch by the end of the decade are expected to produce annual sales in excess of $500 million.

"I would say the ones which have significant potential are certainly PSC, Starlix, Zelmac, then Exelon and Apligraf these are I would say in a bracket above 500 (million dollars sales volume)," Vasella said.
PSC is a drug designed to reverse multidrug resistance in tumour cells resistant to several anti-cancer drugs simultaneously.

Starlix is an insulin secretion stimulant, Zelmac is indicated for irritable bowel syndrome, Exelon for Alzheimer's disease symtoms and Apligraf is a human skin equivalent designed to close difficult to heal wounds.

Kulhoff said the two most promising areas for Novartis seemed to be cancer treatment and central nervous system disorders, such as Alzheimers and Parkinson's diseases, "all areas which have to do with a population growing older".
Societe Generale Equities and Derivatives Research said it was maintaining its view that the stock was an outperformer.

"Novartis also forecast that 37 new products (as opposed to line extensions of existing products) would be launched between 1997 and 2001. We are not aware of any other pharmaceuticals company which will be able to match this roll-out programme," Societe Generale analyst Peter Laing said in a note.
Laing saw Diovan as one of the most promising new drugs and estimated its annual sales potential at some $1 billion.

Diovan, an anti-hypertension drug, would be only the second in a new class of angiotensin II antagonists after Merck's Losartan, marketed at Cozaar, which have fewer side effects than current ACE-inhibitors and calcium antagionists, Laing said.
"These are widely expected to take the market away from ACE-inhibitors and calcium antagonists," Laing said.
Novartis executives also told analysts it had the largest research and development budget in the industry at 2.29 billion Swiss francs in 1996.
